records.name: Malta
records.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first in Europe for LGBTI legal rights every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and "X" gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in the EU, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for SOGIE incidents. The US State Department describes Malta as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence but tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law, with transgender inmates reporting gaps in healthcare and placement procedures.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta: overall index score plus per-category compliance breakdown (asylum, civil society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/speech, equality & non-discrimination, family); Malta has placed first in Europe on the index for a decade.

Equaldex data for Malta: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but Maltese rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Wikipedia overview: Malta is among the world's most progressive - same-sex activity legal since 1973, marriage equality, comprehensive discrimination protections, transgender rights, non-binary birth certificates, intersex rights, conversion-therapy ban, blood-donation equality.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025) by Mary Grace Vella: 'Policing SOGIE hate crime in a liberal state: the case of Malta' - Malta records one of the lowest rates of SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation across the EU27 but a higher share of harassment and online hatred, with low reporting rates to law enforcement; examines 'queering policing'.

University of Malta master's dissertation (2024): 'The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency' - interviews with four current/former trans inmates; obstacles during and after incarceration relate to healthcare, legislation, knowledge/education gaps and post-release life.

ICJ (July 2025): ICJ and partners intervened before the ECtHR in M.S. v. Malta - an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in April 2023 and ordered removed to Bangladesh, where same-sex conduct is criminalised; concerns about risk of persecution and arbitrary detention.

MaltaToday: Transgender Europe applauded Malta for naming gender identity - Malta's pioneering legal recognition of gender identity, which made it a European leader on trans rights (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

records.name: Myanmar
records.summary:
Myanmar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 criminalises same-sex intimacy, reinforced by 'shadow laws' and police discretion (e.g. Section 30(d) of the 1899 Rangoon Police Act used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence). Since the February 2021 coup, risks have intensified sharply - abuses in interrogation and detention reflecting homophobia, transphobia and punitive sexual violence; the UN Special Rapporteur warns of widespread sexual and gender-based violence against women, girls and LGBTQ people.

DVB (Jan 2024): LGBT discrimination on the rise since the 2021 coup - attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse by authorities; the NUG Ministry of Human Rights stated 17 LGBT people were killed and two critically injured since Feb 2021; first-person accounts from trans women protesters.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (Jan 2025): Myanmar's junta banned seven books with LGBTQ+ themes and will take legal action against their publishers, calling them 'obscene' and socially unacceptable - part of the community's long oppression in conservative Myanmar.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025): 'The Silent Struggle' - Myanmar's LGBTQIA+ community under the shadow of the 2024 Conscription Law, based on research by exile-led Queers of Burma Alternative; the law has forced queer individuals into a cycle of fear, discrimination and oppression, with legal frameworks stripping identity (forced into uniforms by assigned gender).
The Guardian (Feb 2016): 'Myanmar's transgender people not just chasing rainbows in fight for equality' - trans activists organising in Yangon despite colonial-era laws and police abuse.
Washington Blade (Nov 2018): a gay man with HIV was charged under Myanmar's sodomy law (Section 377) - demonstrating active enforcement of the colonial-era criminalisation.

HuffPost (Oct 2015): 'Gay People In Myanmar Can't Live Openly. Here's Why' - part of a 10-part series on LGBT rights in Southeast Asia; documents the 2013 Mandalay case where trans women were allegedly forced to strip in public by police; notes nat kadaws (spirit mediums) as trans women or transvestite men within Burmese culture.

records.name: Montenegro
records.summary:
Montenegro is workable for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.
Human Dignity Trust: 'A History of LGBT Criminalisation' - overview of criminalising jurisdictions and strategic litigation (Montenegro context: decriminalised in 1977 under Yugoslavia).

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montenegro: Past and Present' (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; both male and female same-sex activity legal; equal age of consent at 14; same-sex couples lack the legal rights of married couples - historical and cultural context from Ottoman rule to independence.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Podgorica Pride - ~2,000 police guarded ~150 marchers; tear gas used against rock-throwing opponents; organiser Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible'; the march seen as a test of Montenegro's EU human-rights commitments.

PinkNews (Aug 2019): Montenegro's politicians blocked the same-sex partnership law (July 31) despite backing from the governing DPS; conservative Democratic Front deputy Jovan Vucurovic: 'After this law a law on adoption of children by LGBT population will follow'; the Equal Rights Association said LGBT+ people are 'forced to live in hiding'.

CDM/Dan (Dec 2018): the Government defined the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership - granting same-sex couples the same rights as heterosexuals except parenting: no fostering, no adoption; law to enter into force one year after parliamentary adoption.

records.name: Mongolia
records.summary:
Mongolia is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and Ulaanbaatar has an organised community (LGBT Centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections.

Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the LGBT Centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside central Ulaanbaatar.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): notable progress since decriminalisation in 1993 - discrimination based on SOGI prohibited, but no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (protections fragmented); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited; legal gender recognition possible but requires medical intervention (not self-determination); hate-crime and non-discrimination provisions exist in penal and labour codes but enforcement is inconsistent.
ADB publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in Asia and the Pacific - regional comparative overview including Mongolia.

The Establishment (Aug 2018): 'Mongolian Pride: LGBTQ Activism In One Developing Country' by Aubrey Menarndt - profiles Nyamdorj Anaraa, who came out three times (as a lesbian, then a trans man, then a gay trans man); LGBTQ activists leveraging political transition to create progressive change.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): 'Charges in Mongolia LGBT attack hint at changing attitudes' - the far-right group Bosoo Khukh Mongol lured a trans sex worker into a hotel room with a TV station, threatened her and aired the video with commentary accusing LGBT people of paedophilia; charges were brought and investigated as a hate crime - a first; 2017 law changes added hate-crime protections and police training.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: homosexuality has 'virtually no presence, no venues and no activism'; no laws specifically against homosexuality but 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' may still be illegal; a 2008 report described two organisations holding monthly parties for hundreds of members, 'all very furtive'.

records.name: Northern Mariana Islands
records.summary:
A US commonwealth in political union: federal document, immigration and screening policy applies (including 2025–26 marker restrictions), while marriage recognition reached Saipan in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution — recognition exists, and nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression. In 2023 the legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

The policy accounting is nonetheless near-bottom: a comprehensive US equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law in negative territory (sexual-orientation law 'low'), citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection. Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced islands.

sources.claim: Advocates for Trans Equality 'Know Your Rights' guide to US airport security (TSA): body-scanner flags, pat-downs, documentation mismatches, and how to request alternative screening - relevant to the Northern Mariana Islands as a US territory under TSA procedures.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2026): 'US State Revokes Gender-Affirming Identification' — Kansas voids birth certificates and driver's licenses not matching sex assigned at birth; US document-policy context relevant to US territories.

CNMI Public Law 22-32 (signed Jan 2023): amends the Commonwealth Code to provide criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants for hate-motivated crimes - the hate-crimes statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

MAP Equality Profile for the Northern Mariana Islands: LGBTQ policy scores - sexual orientation 4/23 (Low), gender identity -2/26 (Negative), overall 2/49; marriage recognition exists but no second-parent adoption, no family-services nondiscrimination, no assisted-reproduction recognition.
Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBT rights in the Northern Mariana Islands - same-sex marriage legal since 2015 (Obergefell applies), no criminalisation, limited state-level protections.

records.name: Mozambique
records.summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity decriminalised under the new criminal code effective June 2015; courts ruled LGBTIQ organisations can register (2017); employment discrimination based on sexual orientation illegal since 2007 (Law 23/2007) but trans and intersex people not explicitly protected; no legal gender recognition procedure, making trans people particularly vulnerable; societal attitudes broadly neutral but family ostracisation and employment/education challenges occur; during 2024 campaigning the opposition PODEMOS leader pledged to address 'the issue of sexual and ethnic minorities'.

GlobalGayz archive of Mozambique news and reports (2006-2011): the first newspaper article arguing for gay rights (2006), the first national gay-rights seminar, LAMBDA's registration struggles, constitutional-amendment efforts, and refugee risks.

Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016): Afrobarometer survey of Africa's most and least homophobic countries - Mozambique among the most tolerant (56% would welcome a homosexual neighbour), behind Cape Verde (74%) and South Africa (69%).

Global Voices (Nov 2017): after 10 years of legal battles, the Constitutional Council ruled Lambda's status did not violate the constitution - since 2008 the Justice Ministry had ignored Lambda's registration applications; a step toward legal recognition for Mozambique's only LGBT organisation.

The Guardian (June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code scrapped the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda's Carina Capitine: 'The LGBT community is not targeted by violent acts as in some African countries. But we do face discrimination here.'

freshness.fact: Same-sex acts remain legal since the 2015 penal code; note the new 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed since 2007.

records.name: Mauritania
records.summary: Mauritania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents that Mauritania criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under Sharia law.

Cairo 52 country review of Mauritania: gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through 'debauchery', 'heresy' and anti-Sharia provisions - trans people can be apprehended solely for their identity and expression; no gender-affirming healthcare; no legal recognition framework (legislation grounded in Sharia precludes transition); grave lack of information on the trans community.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Mauritania: official assessment - same-sex conduct punishable by death under Sharia-based law; significant societal stigma; no recent executions reported.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Jan 2026), based on Outright International's country overview: the Penal Code provides a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto moratorium in 2021; arrests, detentions and harassment reported; low visibility fuels stigma; Mauritania became a refuge for some Senegalese LGBTIQ people after 2008.

Liberals Mauritania (founded 2014): 'the voice of the freethinkers in Mauritania' - mission to combat mistreatment and prejudice towards non-believers and LGBTQ individuals, eradicate systemic discrimination; publishes on the criminalisation law, apostasy/blasphemy laws, and the story of the first trans woman in Mauritanian media.

records.name: Montserrat
records.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures — the earlier claim of 'archaic criminal provisions on the books' was contradicted by the territory's own sources and has been removed. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

sources.claim: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): the island's gay life was decimated by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 volcano eruption that made the south a wasteland - 'Gays are everywhere but hardly here'; recovery partial.

AP (Jan 2001): Britain scrapped homosexuality laws in its five Caribbean territories (Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat, Turks and Caicos) via Privy Council order after local legislatures refused; religious leaders called it 'totally unacceptable'; the territories appeared resigned to following the order.
